1	# Facts for issue #230 (browser page on the remote port)
2	
3	No spike run; worktree left clean. "W" = WebSearch, "F" = WebFetch. Query text is given per claim.
4	
5	## Settled
6	
7	- iOS 13+ TLS server certificates need the DNS name in subjectAltName (CN ignored), `serverAuth` EKU, and validity of 825 days or less. The page makes no exemption for user-trusted certificates. Evidence: https://support.apple.com/103769 (F). Query: W "iOS 13 requirements for TLS server certificates subjectAltName 825 days manually trusted certificate".
8	- On iOS, a click-through does not carry `wss://`. WebKit bug 41419 is open (NEW, modified 2026-01-12); its 2010 report and a 2011 list thread agree that trusting the certificate made `wss` work and the HTTPS acceptance did not; the maintainer prefers logging to a warning sheet. Evidence: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419 (F); https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-dev/2011-June/017385.html (W). Query: W "WebKit Safari iOS WebSocket wss self-signed certificate exception not applied bug". Agreeing project doc: code-server's iPad guide says Safari blocks WebSockets unless the certificate is installed as a profile, with a matching SAN and `CA:true`, and asks for a domain name rather than an IP: https://github.com/cdr/code-server/blob/v3.7.0/doc/ipad.md (F). Query: W "iOS Safari self-signed certificate warning proceed IP address no subjectAltName wss WebSocket". Two sources agree, so the plan must not rely on a click-through for the socket on iOS.
9	- `.local` names over mDNS reach Mobile Safari on the same network; unicast `.local` DNS is unreliable. Evidence: code-server guide (above, which suggests a `.local` name); https://discussions.apple.com/thread/6555023 (W). Query: W "Safari iOS mDNS .local hostname resolve Bonjour name from Safari". Not tested on a device.
10	- Chrome 58+ ignores CN and needs the SAN for hostname matching. Evidence: https://textslashplain.com/2017/03/10/chrome-deprecates-subject-cn-matching/ (W, one Chromium engineer's post: a lead). Query: W "Chrome 58 deprecate common name certificate hostname matching subjectAltName only announcement". Safari agrees: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=158345 (W). The plan builds the SAN regardless.
11	- A WebSocket that requests a subprotocol must get one back. WHATWG step 11.2 fails the connection if the client sent protocols and the response has no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`; RFC 6455 §4.1 fails it if the server names one the client did not send. Evidence: https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/ (F); https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html (F). Query: W "WebSocket Sec-WebSocket-Protocol browser token subprotocol authentication cookie vs protocol header Safari Chrome" (search gave only lead posts; the standards settle it). The server echoes the token protocol in the 101.
12	- A base64url token is a legal subprotocol value: RFC 7230 `tchar` includes `-` and `_`, and RFC 6455 §4.2.2 takes the value as a `token`, which may not be empty. Evidence: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-3.2.6 (F); RFC 6455 §4.2.2 (F). Standards query only.
13	- The server must validate `Origin` on WebSocket upgrades. RFC 6455 §1.3 says Origin protects against unauthorized cross-origin use; §4.2.2 says a server that does not validate it accepts connections from anywhere. Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455.html (F). The fetch covered the first 100,000 characters only; §10.2 was not read.
14	- Cookies do not isolate by port (RFC 6265 §8.5), so every HTTPS port on one host receives the same cookies; a `Secure` cookie is sent only on secure schemes (§5.4). Evidence: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6265.html (F). Standards query only.
15	- For an https origin, `isSecureContext` depends only on the scheme, not on certificate validity: W3C §3.1 step 3 reads "If origin's scheme is either "https" or "wss", return "Potentially Trustworthy"". Evidence: https://www.w3.org/TR/secure-contexts/ (F). Query: W "W3C secure contexts potentially trustworthy origin https certificate error user bypass". What browsers do after a click-through is Unresolved 2.
16	- `crypto.randomUUID` is secure-context only; `getRandomValues` is not. Evidence: MDN via mirror, https://ligm.univ-eiffel.fr/~forax/MDN/developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Crypto/randomUUID.html (W). Query: W "MDN crypto.randomUUID secure context only available". Generate op ids with `getRandomValues`.
17	- A `SameSite=Strict` cookie can be missing from a WebSocket in a restored Safari tab. WebKit 200345 (open, last comment 2021-07-08): a Strict cookie is sent on a normal load but only the Lax cookie after "Reopen Last Closed Window". WebKit 232666 (Safari 14/15, RESOLVED CONFIGURATION CHANGED, 2021-11-03): Strict cookies are omitted on WebSockets in restored and history-loaded tabs; the maintainer declined to change old versions. Evidence: https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=200345 (F); https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=232666 (F). Query: W "Safari SameSite=Strict cookie WebSocket handshake sent same-site WebKit". The socket must not depend on a Strict cookie alone.
18	- The Stop hook's `last_message` is not on the record. `src/adapters/hooks.rs:196` builds `EventKind::Stopped { last_message, pending }`, `src/ports/events.rs:24` carries it, and the core reads only `pending` (`src/core/events.rs:132`). `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs`) has no excerpt field. Tree.
19	- `WATCH_CAP` is 128 (`src/content.rs:42`). Tree.
20	- No test under `tests/` builds `RemoteRequest` or `RemoteReply` as a literal. They are built in `src/adapters/remote.rs:506` and `src/app.rs` (`:1664`, `:1679`, `:2365`, `:2371`, `:2376`). Tree.
21	- `PairingInvite` is used in 12 Swift files: four under `client/Sources` (`switchboard-remote/main.swift`, `SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift`, `SwitchboardClientCore/ConnectionManager.swift`, `SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift`) and eight under `client/Tests`. Tree.
22	
23	## Unresolved
24	
25	1. Does iOS Safari offer a click-through for an untrusted self-signed certificate on a bare IP? Kurento says iOS "will outright reject untrusted self-signed certs, instead of showing a security warning" (https://doc-kurento.readthedocs.io/en/stable/knowledge/selfsigned_certs.html, F). A search result describes a "Show Details / Visit this website" path, from a third-party manual rather than Apple (W "iPhone Safari 'This Connection Is Not Private' visit this website self-signed certificate local network iOS 17 Show Details"). Sources conflict and the iOS version is unknown. Build to: no dependency on the click-through. Owner: O1.
26	2. Click-through on Chrome and Firefox for a no-SAN certificate on an IP, and whether `isSecureContext` is `true` after one. Query: W "window.isSecureContext after proceeding past certificate error interstitial Chrome secure context". Only a 2017 secondhand W3C-list report says yes. Build to: SAN in the certificate, and a `getRandomValues` fallback. Owner: O2.
27	3. Does a click-through persist across launches? Query: W "Chrome certificate exception proceed anyway persist across browser restart session only self-signed". Chrome: no source. Firefox: a Mozilla bug shows "Permanently store this exception" checked by default (a lead). Build to: treat the exception as lost at each launch.
28	4. Do Chrome and Firefox send `SameSite=Strict` cookies on same-origin WebSocket handshakes? Only WebKit sources found (Settled above). Build to: the token travels in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, so the socket does not depend on this.
29	5. Does `Secure` work on an IP-address host in browsers? RFC 6265 §5.4 allows it for a secure scheme; no browser source found. One unanswered Apple Developer Forums post reports a Safari non-resend of an HttpOnly+Secure+SameSite=Strict cookie set on a 101: https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/104488 (F). Build to: the cookie name carries `server_id`, and nothing depends on the cookie for the socket.
30	6. Connections per host from iOS Safari. Query: W "Chrome max connections per host HTTP/1.1 six parallel connections Safari WebKit per-host limit". Chrome's 6 comes from secondary sources. The WebKit Mac scheduler source returned 404 to F (https://opensource.apple.com/source/WebKit2/WebKit2-7537.71/NetworkProcess/mac/NetworkResourceLoadSchedulerMac.mm.auto.html). Build to: a small page connection count, and measure (O5).
31	7. rcgen 0.14 defaults. Query: W "rcgen CertificateParams default not_after 4096 self_signed KeyPair from_pem rcgen 0.14"; F https://docs.rs/rcgen/0.14.10/rcgen/struct.CertificateParams.html. The docs give no defaults, and the crate source could not be read from this session. The tree's "year 4096" comment (`src/adapters/remote.rs:91`) is unverified. Build to: set `not_before`, `not_after` (≤825 days), SANs, `serverAuth` EKU and `is_ca` explicitly. Whether `KeyPair::from_pem` exists for a reissue over the stored key is also unverified; compile it before relying on it.
32	8. Does `history.replaceState` remove the query from Safari's history menu, "recently closed", or iCloud tab sync, or does the browser record the URL before the script runs (including Chrome and Firefox)? Query: W "history.replaceState URL query removed from Safari history recently closed tabs iCloud tab sync before script runs". Nothing on these. One WebKit report says `replaceState` may add history-menu entries, and a maintainer replied that Safari decides what the menu shows (https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=58072, W). Build to: the code is single-use, refused after its first attempt, and expires with the window (five minutes); a leaked URL then grants nothing.
33	
34	## For the owner
35	
36	- O1 (Decision 1): On an iPhone, does Safari offer a click-through for the host's certificate on its IP, and does the page then load and fetch? Does a profile with a SAN certificate (CA:true, serverAuth, ≤825 days, full trust enabled) let `wss://` connect? Either branch works if the plan ships the profile download for the socket and falls back to polling `/api/v1/` when the socket fails, so no branch depends on the click-through.
37	- O2 (Decision 1): Does `window.isSecureContext` read `true` on the device after the click-through? If yes, use `crypto.randomUUID`; if no, use `getRandomValues`. Both work with the fallback.
38	- O3 (Decision 2): On the device, does a token in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` survive reopening Safari and history navigation? The protocol route does not depend on cookies, so it works either way.
39	- O4 (Decisions 1 and 3): Does the browser keep the pairing URL in history or tab sync after `replaceState`? Either answer is covered by the single-use code and five-minute expiry in Unresolved 8.
40	- O5 (Decision 4): How many connections does iOS Safari open to one host on a page load, and how long does it keep them? Measure before the pool size is fixed.

1	# Issue #230: a browser page on the remote port, investigation notes
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (84 lines, nothing about the remote port;
4	its lesson is the action/effect core, a fake for every port, and "spike
5	risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
6	boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
7	plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
8	7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.
9	
10	## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back
11	
12	- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
13	  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
14	  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
15	  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
16	  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
17	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
18	  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
19	  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
20	  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
21	  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
22	  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
23	  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.
24	- **Rehydration** is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded { identity, devices,
25	  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
26	  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request
27	  (`authenticate`, `src/app.rs:3125-3153`; `device_by_token`,
28	  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
29	  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
30	  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
31	  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).
32	- **The pairing window is not durable** (`PairingWindow` in core state:
33	  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/
34	  `PairingFailed`/`Paired`, `src/core/remote.rs:46-73`). The QR is built
35	  in the UI from it (`src/ui/remote.rs:155-173`). Changing JSON to a URL
36	  is a change to that `json!` call and to the "Copy invite" text (`:199-206`),
37	  not to any record.
38	- **The page itself is not a record.** It is static bytes compiled in
39	  (`include_str!`). On the device, what persists is the token, plus
40	  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
41	  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per
42	  host. The host keeps nothing new per browser beyond the device record.
43	- **Identity** (`identity.json`, `Identity` at `src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`,
44	  `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` at `:17`). It holds the certificate
45	  (base64 DER) and `spki_sha256`. The certificate is made by
46	  `make_identity` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`) with
47	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::<String>::new())`: **no subjectAltName at
48	  all**, a CN of `Switchboard <server_id>`, rcgen's default validity
49	  (the comment says `not_after` is the year 4096), and no EKU set
50	  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
51	  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
52	  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
53	  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused
54	  (the SPKI is the same, §5). But the certificate is stored in
55	  `identity.json`, so reissuing it means writing that file, and an
56	  address that moves would need another reissue.
57	
58	## What the code does today, piece by piece
59	
60	### The listener (`src/adapters/remote.rs`)
61	
62	- `read_request` (`:444-513`) keeps the method, the path, the query
63	  (undecoded), the body, `bearer` (`Authorization: Bearer`, `:487-491`)
64	  and `upgrade` (`Sec-WebSocket-Key` when `Upgrade: websocket`,
65	  `:492-495`). It throws away every other header. **It does not read
66	  `Cookie`, `Origin`, `User-Agent`, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, `Host`,
67	  `If-None-Match` or `Accept`.** Either token transport in decision 2
68	  needs a new `RemoteRequest` field. That struct is in
69	  `src/adapters/remote.rs:359-372`, which is not under `ports/`, but
70	  `tests/remote.rs` builds requests and should be checked.
71	- `respond` (`:530-552`) always writes `Content-Type: application/json`
72	  and `Connection: keep-alive`, nothing else. It has no CSP, no
73	  Cache-Control, no Set-Cookie and no other content type. `RemoteReply`
74	  (`:388-393`) is `{status, body, authenticated}`. Static files and a
75	  cookie on `/pair` therefore need `RemoteReply` (or a separate
76	  connection-thread path) to carry headers. `respond_upgrade`
77	  (`:519-527`) writes no `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`. A browser that offered
78	  a subprotocol fails the handshake if the server does not echo one
79	  (that is a question below, not checked).
80	- Pools and windows: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`
81	  (`:567-568`). A stream past the 4 is dropped at accept (`:699-706`). A
82	  connection moves pools only when a reply says `authenticated: true`
83	  (`:834-849`). `HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT` is 5 s (`:570`), and the first
84	  request line has the same deadline. `IDLE_TIMEOUT` is 30 s (`:573`).

risky technology first"), docs/remote-client.md §§0–5, design.md "Trust
boundary" (l.219) and the start of "Remote client (2026-10-12)" (l.3107),
plus the code below. Line numbers are as they are in this worktree at
7fe8949. There is no `web/` directory yet.

## The record first: what is on disk, and how it comes back

- **No new record kind and no `model.rs` change is needed.** A browser is
  one more `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`: `id`, `name`,
  `scope`, `token_sha256`, `created`, `last_seen`) in
  `<data dir>/devices.json`. That file is a bare `Vec<PairedDevice>`
  with no schema version (`RemoteFiles::load_devices`/`save_devices`,
  `src/adapters/remote.rs:80-86`), written atomically by
  `Effect::SaveDevices` (`src/core/remote.rs:121-125`). The name comes
  from `/pair`'s `device_name` (`src/app.rs:3650-3655`), cut to 64 chars
  in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166-175`). So "Safari on
  iPhone" can be the page's own `device_name` with no host change. If
  the plan wants a `kind` (browser or native) on the device, it is an
  additive `#[serde(default)]` field in a file that has no version.

  rotated }` (`src/core/remote.rs:22-30`) puts the devices back at
  launch. A token is checked by hash against them on every request

  `src/core/remote.rs:145-147`). Revoke (`RevokeDevice`,
  `src/core/remote.rs:86-92`) and scope change (`:93-100`) apply on the
  next request, and revoke closes the device's socket (test
  `revoke_closes_the_devices_socket`, `tests/remote.rs:2892`).

  code, scope, `until`, failures; `OpenPairing`/`ClosePairing`/

  not to any record.

  whatever the page keeps to say "identity changed". Decision 2 picks
  where that is. The browser also keeps its certificate exception per

  explicitly. The native clients pin the SPKI and ignore names, so this
  never mattered. A browser checks names and validity. Changing the
  certificate (adding SANs for the LAN address or a `.local` name, or a
  bounded validity) changes nothing the pin sees if the key is reused

## 4. Rust host

### 4.1 Implementation

- **No Tokio.** The host is std threads and `mpsc`; the core is owned by `SwitchboardApp` and every state change is a dispatch on the frame thread. The remote port follows the `ControlSocket` shape: an accept thread per listener, one thread per connection, each request handed over a channel to the frame, answered by the same `serve` path in `app.rs` (`serve_pending` runs before every frame, hidden ones included), the reply sent back on the connection's channel. A second runtime inside an egui app buys nothing for a handful of connections.
- **The frame does core state only.** A metadata request (a view, a command) is answered on the frame as the control port is. A content request (conversation, screen, run output, file) takes two steps: the frame answers with the **handle and the redaction policy** (the transcript path and resume handle, the pane's host id, the run's log path, the file's root and relative path, plus the secret values to mask and the policy fingerprint), and one **content worker thread** does the read, the parse, the mask, the version check and the serialization from a queue of such requests (one at a time, so one large parse is in memory at once; Spike 22 measured 575 MB peak for the largest transcript), then sends one small action back to the frame to record the version it observed (§4.4), and the connection thread writes the reply. The watch poll (§4.4) runs through the same worker. A multi-megabyte transcript, a 768 KiB file or a slow Keychain call therefore costs the worker its time and the asking connection its wait, never a frame. The handle is read under the frame's authority, so a record removed or rebound between the two steps makes the worker's version action a no-op and the reply carries the handle it read from.
- **Bounds.** The port is one user's few devices, and the limits say so:
  - at most 16 connections in total and 4 unauthenticated ones; a further accept is closed at once. The 4 are a separate pool: an unauthenticated flood fills its own slots and never a paired client's;
  - `/pair` is answered at most six times a minute per listener and `/info` sixty; past that the connection thread answers 429 without reaching the frame;
  - a TLS handshake and the first request line each within 5 s, a request body within 10 s, a write within 10 s; a connection that misses a deadline is closed;
  - one request in flight per connection (HTTP/1.1, no pipelining);
  - the frame drains at most 8 remote requests per pass, in arrival order, the rest waiting on the channel; the channel is bounded at 64 and a full channel answers 503 from the connection thread without reaching the frame; a frame-side request is a view or a handle lookup and takes microseconds, so the count is the bound;
  - each WebSocket subscriber has an event queue of 256; when it fills, the subscriber is sent `resync_required` and closed, never silently trimmed (§4.4);
  - the watch set (§4.4) is capped at 128 keys for the whole port; past the cap the least recently read key is evicted silently, since a read of an evicted key always works and re-enters it.
- Preferred crates: a blocking HTTP/1.1 server over `std::net::TcpListener` (hand-rolled or `tiny_http`), `tungstenite` for WebSocket, `rustls` with `rcgen` for the per-installation certificate, and `mdns-sd` (or the system `dns-sd` through a small macOS adapter) for Bonjour. All of it in `src/adapters/remote.rs` behind a `ports::remote` trait with a fake, and all of it must compile on Linux CI (Bonjour may be a `cfg(target_os = "macos")` adapter with a no-op elsewhere). **Spike 22 (§10) decides the exact crates before any of this is built.**
- Handlers are thin: HTTP request → auth and scope check → allowlist → `wire::Request` → `serve` → redaction → `wire::Reply` → HTTP response. No session or transcript logic lives in the adapter.
- Only the instance holding the store lock listens (as the control port does); a read-only instance refuses to bind.
- Bind to loopback by default until remote access is explicitly enabled in Settings. For LAN access, bind the chosen interface and require pairing.
- Configurable port in `identity.json` (§3.1), default `43187`, overridable with `SWITCHBOARD_REMOTE_PORT` (a dev aid, documented in the README) so two instances can run on one machine; `0` picks a free one, which the tests use.
- Advertise `_switchboard._tcp` via Bonjour only while listening on a non-loopback interface. TXT records carry the protocol major version (`v`), the display name (`name`) and the `server_id` (`id`, so a client matches a record to a known server before it connects); never a token, never key material. The instance name is the display name with a short id suffix, so two installations on one machine stay distinct.
- If Switchboard closes, the port goes away. A standalone daemon is not in scope.

### 4.2 API conventions

- Version prefix: `/api/v1`.
- JSON request and response bodies. Timestamps as milliseconds since the epoch, matching the wire crate (`last_stop_at_ms`); the client formats them.
- The wire crate's views are the response schemas. New views are added to `switchboard-control` additively (it stays std + serde only, and Dispatch keeps compiling).
- Standard error shape: `{ "error": { "code": "...", "message": "..." } }`, with `wire::Reply::Failed` mapped onto it.
- **Every response** carries the host's `epoch` and `revision` (§4.4) in an envelope: `{ "epoch": "...", "revision": n, "body": ... }`. The revision is the one at which the body's **content version** was observed (§4.4, "Content versions"), not merely the counter at the time of the reply. The client keeps one held revision per resource key (a session's metadata, its conversation, its screen, one run's output, one file are separate keys) and applies a reply only if its revision is at or past the held one, so an older reply arriving after a newer one is dropped and fetching a session's metadata never invalidates a valid conversation page.
- **Caps.** The serialized, masked body of any reply is at most 1 MiB, envelope included, enforced on the output bytes. The rule per kind:
  - **collections** (`projects`, `spaces`, `sets`, `sessions`, `runs`, a set's pins, `waiting`) are answered **whole, in one reply, never paged and never cut**. They are small: a data directory holds hundreds of records at most, and a project's session list with every string bounded as below is under 100 KiB at that scale. A collection reply is one snapshot of its membership at one revision, which is what makes a cached member's removal safe: a member missing from a whole reply at a revision at or past the one it was learned at is gone. The 1 MiB cap is enforced on the serialized reply as everywhere; a collection that would exceed it is a bug in the bounds, answered `too_large` and logged, not paged around.
  - **metadata views**, in a collection and standing alone, are bounded field by field, after masking: `notes` at 4 KiB in a collection and 64 KiB standing alone, `name`, `waiting_reason`, `cwd` and every other free-text string at 4 KiB, each cut marked in a `truncated` list of field names; no field is left unbounded. A client that wants a session's full notes reads the session alone.
  - **conversation** pages stop at `limit` turns or at the cap with `next`; a turn larger than 256 KiB is cut and marked (§4.3).
  - **last response** and **run output** are cut from the front (older text dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
  - **file content** is sent whole or not at all: the port's file limit is 768 KiB of source bytes, and a larger pinned file answers `too_large` with its size. The source limit is not a guarantee of fit: JSON escaping can double a file of quotation marks and masking can lengthen text, so the limit is enforced once more on the masked, serialized reply, and a file that exceeds it there answers `too_large` too, naming the serialized size. The client says so on the card.
  - **screen** is bounded by `lines` (at most 200) and, after masking, by bytes: text over 256 KiB is cut from the top (older lines dropped) and marked `truncated: true`.
- A command is **accepted** when `serve` returns; its outcome arrives through events and the session's state. For `session.send` there is no completion signal beyond the next `Stop` hook event on that record (§4.5).
- Document payload schemas with examples; generate the Swift `Codable` types from the Rust views (serde shapes) and keep a fixture test on both sides.

### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists `scope` among its capabilities. The point is the wire: hundreds of worker sessions on a host, which the headset fetched one project at a time, are now neither fetched nor announced.
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based rule-set change all surface without anyone naming them. The fingerprint is a hash over the view's serialized bytes **with its time-derived fields held at zero**: `quiet_secs` is computed from the clock in `session_view` and would move every pass, so the view gains an additive `last_activity_ms` the client derives quiet from, and the quiet **state** (the card's word moving to idle) is what the diff sees. Collections carry the membership revision of §4.2, bumped only when the member id set moves. The hash is cheap at this scale (hundreds of records); the spike measures it (§10).
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged:
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff pass (the `env.*` actions are dispatches), which emits `changed` for every watched content key of the affected project without waiting for a read.
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no read for a minute is dropped too. A read of a key not in the set still answers and still versions correctly, since the version is checked on every read; what eviction costs is the `changed` event until the next read, which the client's periodic refetch of a visible view covers.

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. A visible content view also refetches on its own every thirty seconds, which is what covers a key the host evicted from the set.

**The conversation cache** moves from `UiState` to `SwitchboardApp` as one of the content caches, keyed by record id, resume handle and content version, read by the session view and the port alike; `UiState` keeps a reference, not a copy. This is a frontend change (the session, card and workflow views read the cache), so it is its own commit before any port code, Milestone A0 (§10), with the app behaving identically. This, the diff and the worker handoff are the changes to the app outside the adapter, and §12.6 says why they are required.

**Subscribe first, then snapshot.** A client connecting to a host:

1. opens the WebSocket and waits for `hello {epoch, revision}` (events start flowing at once and are buffered by the client);
2. fetches the snapshots it needs, each reply carrying its own `revision`;
3. applies the buffered events: an event whose `revision` is past a snapshot's `revision` invalidates that resource and is refetched; the rest were already in the snapshot;
4. enables commands.

Because the subscriber is registered on the frame thread before any later pass can bump `revision`, a metadata snapshot is taken on that thread with the revision it carries, and a content reply is stamped on that thread when the worker's version action lands (the same moment its `changed` would be emitted, so the event and the reply name one revision), no change can fall between a subscription and a snapshot. Several snapshots in flight are each reconciled against the buffer by their own revision; events that arrive during a refetch are reconciled the same way, which is why the client never clears its buffer until step 4. A resource named by an event the client has never seen is fetched. If `epoch` differs from the one the client holds (the host restarted), every cached item is stale and is refetched. There is no retained-event replay: a `resync_required` is the only answer to a gap, and events are never durable.

### 4.5 Commands

- `send`, `resume` and `trust` are authenticated actions under `control` scope against one owning server and session.
- The client makes a UUID operation id per command and sends it as the wire `op`.
- **Logged before run.** Today `operations.log` gets a request line only for creations, and the reply line after the command ran; `serve` skips a command only when a reply line exists. That leaves a crash between sending keys and appending the reply as a repeat on retry. The port closes that gap for every non-replayable command (`Class::NonReplayable`: `session.send`, `session.resume`): `serve` appends the request line **before** dispatch, and a failed append refuses the command without running it. On arrival, an op with a request line and no reply line is answered `interrupted` and **not run again**; an op with a reply line is answered from it. `session.trust` is `Idempotent` on the wire and needs neither.
- The client's rule per `/ops/{op}` status:
  - `done`: use the reply;
  - `interrupted`: the host started it and the outcome is unknown; never resubmit; show the session's current state and let the user decide;
  - `unknown`: the host never received it (nothing was logged, and the frame answers queued requests in arrival order, so a request that had reached the frame before the status query has a line); resubmitting with the same op is safe.
  A timeout on a command is followed by a status query, never by a blind resend.
- `send` puts keys into the pane, as the app's own message box does. "Accepted" means the keys were sent. Progress is the record's state: `PromptSubmitted`, then working, then `Stop` with the new last response. A send to a pane sitting at Claude Code's folder trust question is accepted but goes nowhere until `trust` answers it; the session view carries `trust_question`, and the client shows the same "Trust this folder" button the app shows.
- `resume` on a not-running agent is user-initiated, so allowed, but the client confirms it ("Resume spends a turn") before sending; the host never resumes on its own.
- Failures name the reason: not running, not resumable, unknown record, scope missing, pairing revoked, log unavailable.
- **A new session (2026-10-19).** `POST projects/{id}/sessions` under `control` opens a session in the project, through the same `session.new` the CLI and Dispatch use, with the body's `op` as the key: `{op, name, kind, cwd, prompt}`, `kind` one of `claude`, `codex` or `shell` (a command or a service is not opened from a device), `cwd` the project's root when absent and otherwise a directory under it, relative or absolute, refused `bad_request` when it steps out of the root or is not a directory, so a device never opens a shell elsewhere on the disk; `prompt` is an agent's first message, on its command line as the CLI puts it, so the agent is already working when the device opens the window. The reply is the command body with `made: [{kind: "session", id}]`; `/ops/{op}` carries `made` too, so a creation whose reply was lost still names its record. `info` lists `create`. The client offers it on a host that is connected, paired under `control` and serves `create`: a plus button on the Sessions tab and "New session in this project" on a listed session, opening a sheet with the host, the project by workspace, the kind, a name (the kind's word and a count when none is typed), a directory and the first message; Start posts it, reads the project's sessions again and opens the new session's window.

**The draft.** An agent session's prompt on the host is its Prompt Box editor (design.md, "Prompt Box status"), one document with undo, the live utterance as a provisional span, voice commands and the AI pass. A device does not keep a prompt of its own: it reads the editor's draft and works on it, so dictation from the headset, dictation at the desk and typing on either meet in one text, and a prompt begun on one device can be finished on the other. The editor exists whether or not the session is drawn on the host, as it does for a card's microphone.

- `GET sessions/{id}/draft` (any paired device) answers `{draft: {text, live, status, status_text, can_undo, can_redo, ai, busy}}`: the rendered text, the byte range of the utterance still being recognized or null, the editor's status (`idle`, `listening`, `finishing`, `degraded`, `error`) with its reason, whether undo and redo apply, whether the host has an `OpenAI` key for the AI pass, and whether a pass is running. Only an agent session has a draft (`no_draft` otherwise). The host emits `changed {draft, id}` for an editor whose draft moved, fingerprinted a few times a second while a subscriber is connected, and a device holding the draft re-reads it; no watch is needed, since the editor is the host's own state rather than a source the worker polls.
- `POST sessions/{id}/draft` (control) applies one of the editor's tools and answers with the draft as it stands: `{action: "replace", text}` sets the text whole (what the device typed; last writer wins, one person), `undo`, `redo`, `clear`, `clean_up` (the AI pass, refused `failed` when the host has no key), `delete_sentence`, `delete_paragraph`, and `{action: "send", op}`, which takes the draft's text to the pane exactly as `session.send` does, under the device's op as the key, and clears the editor when it went; a repeat of a send that went is answered from the log. A send of an empty draft is refused.
- `POST sessions/{id}/dictation` (control) carries `{session, events}`: the device's recognizer session, a number the device picks apart from the host's own, and its speech events in order, each `{sequence, kind, utterance, revision, text}` with `kind` one of `started`, `voice_started`, `partial`, `final`, `voice_ended`, `stopped`. The host feeds them to the editor as its own recognizer's events: `started` puts the editor's status at listening, a partial is the provisional span revised in place, a final commits the utterance at its anchor, `stopped` returns the status to idle. At most 256 events of 16 KiB each per request. The reply is the draft as it stands, so the device sees its words land without waiting for the event. The device segments speech into utterances itself (the Apple recognizer starts over after a pause and closes an utterance by re-sending its words later); the editor keeps the document. Two recognizers into one editor (the desk's and the headset's) are kept apart by their session numbers.

"Waiting on you" on a card includes reasons set from outside: Dispatch marks a session through `session.waiting` when one of its tickets needs a decision. `SessionView.waiting_reason` is already on the wire; the client shows it. #### 4.7 Tickets

The ticket view on a device (2026-10-17) reads Dispatch through the Switchboard port, not Dispatch's own socket, which only the Mac reaches: the port serves what the app already holds from its two-second status poll, so a device costs the runner nothing. `GET dispatch/tickets` is the core's `TicketListing` (`src/core/tickets.rs`): `connected` (a runner answered the last poll; without one the tickets are the last seen), the `projects` with a pipeline (slots, running, pending, waiting on me, the queue, the supervisor's session id), and the `tickets` by project then oldest first, never the runner's write order. Each ticket is a summary: source, state and reason, the current stage's name among the `stages`, `standing` worded exactly as the Mac's page words it (`1 waiting on you`, `plan running`, `parked: <reason>`, `held: <why>`), `waits` and `urgent` as the page colours it, `current_session` and `root_project`, and every decision with its question, options, recommendation, `multiple`, state, answer and `needs_note`. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}` adds the body (bounded at the notes cap), the attempts with the session each ran in and the pull request it is bound to, the lanes by branch, and the holds; paths stay on the Mac. The collection is one resource, `tickets` with an empty id, fingerprinted with everything else: a decision made or answered, a stage moved, or the runner coming or going is one `changed` frame, to every subscriber.

Two commands under `control`, each the Mac's own action and so Dispatch's own call: `decide` takes `{decision, answer, note?}` (the decision's id; for a `multiple` decision the options joined by commas) and is checked against the last status before anything runs (the decision pending, every option among the decision's, a note where the option needs one), and `resume` a parked ticket. The reply is deferred until Dispatch answers the call, through the same channel the content worker answers on: `{decision}` or `{ticket}` on success, the runner's reason as `failed` or `not_found`, `dispatch_off` (503) when no runner answers. A decision already answered as asked is answered again from the record, so a device that lost the reply repeats at no cost; one answered otherwise is `answered` (409). `info` lists `tickets` among the capabilities, and a client treats a host without it as having no tickets.

The files of each attempt (2026-10-18) ride on the single-ticket read: `TicketAttempt.files` names each artifact the attempt wrote (its notes, a plan, a review summary), the log of the stage's checks, each review round's findings and response, and every file of its evidence directory, with a `kind`, whether it is `inline` text or an `image`, and for evidence its size and time. A file is named by a `key`, a hash of its path, so the path stays on the Mac; a secret artifact is listed as `secret` and never read. `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/files/{key}` answers `{key, text}` for text, through the Mac's own `DispatchReadArtifact` (so Dispatch's refusals, of a secret or of a file outside the ticket, are the device's answer, and a text the Mac already holds for the ticket as it stands is answered from its cache), bounded at 256 KiB; for an evidence image it answers `{key, media, data}` with the bytes as base64, read from the disk here, up to 700 KiB (`too_large`, 413, beyond that). `GET dispatch/tickets/{id}/events` is the ticket's event log as the Mac's cache holds it after its `DispatchReadEvents`, `{events, last, unavailable}`, served from the cache while the ticket has not changed; both reads are deferred until Dispatch answers, as the commands are. `close` is the third command, refused as `not_closable` (409) unless the status says the ticket may be closed. The attempt also carries its `checks` (head and exit) and its review `rounds`. `info` lists `evidence` for all of this, and a client shows a host without it the files by name only.

The client scans or types both; it connects, compares the hash of the key it is actually talking to with the one it was given, and only when they match sends `/pair {code, device_name, spki_sha256}`. A client without a camera (visionOS gives an app none) pairs from the host's Bonjour record instead: it resolves the record, reads `/info` under no trust, shows the key the host presented in the dialog's short form for the owner to compare by eye, and pins that key for the pairing, so the typed code reaches only the host whose key the owner checked; a substituted certificate shows its own key on the device, where the owner sees it differ. The host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request through a substituted certificate fails even if the code reached it. ### 4.4 WebSocket events

Envelope:

```json
{
  "server_id": "uuid",
  "epoch": "uuid",
  "revision": 1042,
  "type": "changed",
  "resource": {"kind": "session", "id": "record-uuid"},
  "at_ms": 1760220000000
}
```

Event types:

- `hello {epoch, revision}`: the first frame on every subscription.
- **Scope.** A listing leaves out the records Dispatch made for its own use: a ticket's project with everything in it, and a worker session (the planner, an implementer, a reviewer) in any project, told by the `<ticket>-<nonce>` form of the op they were made under (`switchboard_control::is_dispatch_worker_op`). A supervisor's records (`sup-…`) and the owner's own are listed as ever, and a worker record is still read by its id, which is how the ticket view to come will reach them. `?scope=all` on `projects`, `sessions`, `waiting` and on the `events` subscription lists them and announces them; a plain subscription gets no `project`, `sessions`, `session` or `runs` frame about one. `info` lists
- `changed {kind, id}` with the **metadata kinds** `project`, `space`, `set`, `session`; the **content kinds** `conversation`, `screen`, `run_output` (`id` = `record/n`), `file` (a pinned file, `id` = `project_id/path`); and the collection kinds `projects`, `spaces`, `sets` (with the space's id), `sessions` (with the project's id), `runs` (with the record's id), `waiting`, emitted when a collection's member id set moves and answered by refetching the collection whole; a global collection's `id` is the empty string. Each kind is its own resource key on the client (§4.2); a member fetched as part of its collection holds the collection's revision until it is read alone.
- `removed {kind, id}`: the resource is gone; the client drops it and marks any window on it "removed on <server>".
- `watching {kind, id}`: the answer to a `watch` frame (below).
- `resync_required`: sent before the host closes a subscriber whose queue overflowed; the client reconnects and refetches everything.

**What produces events.** The host has no event bus, and a save is not a reliable sign of a visible change: working sets save through `SaveViews`, Claude Code's trust question (`PromptSeen`) and a Codex pane going quiet (`HostListed`) change what a card says with no save at all. So the port does not watch for saves. Revision and events come from three places in `app.rs`:

1. **The read-model diff, after every pass.** After every `dispatch` and after every polling pass (`HostListed`, the hook log, `Tick`), the app recomputes a cheap per-resource fingerprint of each exported metadata read model (`SessionView`, `SetView` with its members, `ProjectView`, `SpaceView`, `waiting`) and compares it with the previous pass's. One `changed` per resource whose fingerprint moved, one `removed` per resource that vanished, one `changed` per collection whose membership moved, and `revision` bumped once per pass that emitted anything. The diff is the gate, not the effect list, so a set rename, a pin edit, a trust-question transition, a quiet-state transition and a time-based r
2. **Content versions, assigned where content is read.** Conversation text, pane text, run output and pinned files are mutable outside the core and can change between two reads inside one poll interval, so a content reply's revision cannot come from the counter alone. Every content read goes through a per-key **content cache** in `SwitchboardApp`, whose bookkeeping lives on the frame and whose reads run on the connection or worker thread (§4.1). The cache holds, per key, the **source version** and the **policy fingerprint of the owning project (§4.3)** it last served, with the revision it was assigned. The source version per kind, chosen so that no change the host can see leaves it unchanged
   - **transcript**: size and mtime. Claude Code's JSONL only appends, Switchboard never edits one, and `/clear` or a discard rebinds the record to another file, so a growing size is a reliable version and a same-size rewrite does not occur;
   - **pinned file**: inode, ctime and size, read from the descriptor the walk ends on. No user tool preserves ctime, so an editor that rewrites in place, a same-size rewrite, and a replace-by-rename (a new inode) all move it;
   - **run output**: inode, ctime and size of the run's log. A log truncated and regrown to the same length has a new ctime; a rotated one a new inode;
   - **screen**: a hash of the pane text, as today.
   When either the source version or the policy fingerprint differs from what the cache holds, the worker's reply carries the new content and the frame, on the worker's version action, bumps `revision`, emits `changed {content kind, id}`, and stores the new version with that revision; the reply is stamped with that revision. **Two different content versions never share a revision for one key within an epoch**, and two reads of unchanged content return the same bytes and the same revision. The policy is resolved before the read; a resolution failure refuses the reply and leaves the cache untouched, so no earlier masked bytes stand in for the answer. A policy change is also noticed by the diff
3. **The watch poll.** The port keeps a **watch set**: every content key any subscriber has asked to watch, plus every content key read in the last minute. Independently of the local view, every two seconds a worker thread checks each watched key's source version (a `stat`, or a pane snapshot for `screen`; never a parse) and, for a key that moved, reads it through the content cache, which is what emits the `changed`. The local session view reads its conversation through the same cache (an unmasked variant; §4.3), so the two polls share work rather than duplicate it. The set is capped at 128 keys (§4.1); past that the least recently read key is dropped, and a key with no subscriber and no rea

**Watch frames.** A client sends `watch {kind, id}` when the first view instance on a content key opens and `unwatch` when the last one closes; the client keeps a reference count per key so closing one of two windows on a session changes nothing on the host. The host answers `watching` once the key is in its set, and the client fetches the initial content only after that, so the first snapshot's revision is covered by the poll from then on. A watch is never refused. On reconnect, after `hello`, the client resends every watch with a nonzero count before it snapshots. # Plan: a web control surface on the remote port (issue #230)

One commit. The app runs at every step; the order below is the order to build in. File and line references are to this worktree at 7fe8949. "Facts" is the facts file; a line under Settled is cited as such, a line under Unresolved or For the owner is named where the decision is made, and the default on that decision is the design that works whichever way the answer goes.

## Where this departs from the issue

- **"The page shows the one-line excerpt the card shows."** There is no such field on the wire. `SessionView` (`control/src/lib.rs:637-688`) has `card`, `waiting_reason`, `last_stop_at_ms` and no excerpt; the Stop hook's `last_message` is built at `src/adapters/hooks.rs:196` and the core reads only `pending` (`src/core/events.rs:132`). The plan adds no read model. The list shows the card word, the waiting reason and the age; for waiting sessions only (at most eight) it fetches `last-response` once, unwatched, and shows its first line. This is the headset's method (`client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:149-163`).
- **"The device's scope in the header."** `docs/remote-client.md` §5 says the host answers each later request with the device's scope. It does not: scope leaves the host only in the `/pair` reply (`src/app.rs:3662`), and nothing says it afterwards. A scope changed in the dialog would never reach the page. The plan adds one authenticated read, `GET /api/v1/device`.
- **"'Revoked' said plainly."** `authenticate` (`src/app.rs:3127-3153`) refuses a revoked token and a never-paired one with the same code, `unauthorized`. The plan does not change the code. The page keeps a non-secret marker (`server_id`, `device_id`) in `localStorage`; a 401 with a marker is "revoked", a 401 without one is "not paired".
- **"Any path outside `/api/v1/` is refused."** True, but only on the frame, after the request took an inbox slot (`src/app.rs:3023`). The static paths are answered on the connection thread instead, so a page load costs the frame nothing.
- **§5: "the host refuses a pairing whose `spki_sha256` is not its own, so a relayed request … fails."** That holds for a client that pins the key it talks to. For a browser the `spki_sha256` in the POST comes from the page, and under a relay the page is the impostor's. The key in the URL catches a genuine page reaching a wrong genuine host (a second installation at the address, a rotated key); it does not catch a relay. §5 gets this said in its own words.
- **Facts, Unresolved 8: "the code is single-use, refused after its first attempt."** The tree does less. The window closes on the first *successful* pairing (`src/core/remote.rs:57-61`); a failed attempt counts and the window closes at the third (`:49-56`, `PAIRING_ATTEMPTS`). So a pairing URL that leaks stays valid until it is used, three attempts fail, or five minutes pass. The plan keeps those rules (they are the spec's, §5) and says so in the spec instead of claiming more. The page compares keys before it posts, so a mismatch never counts against the window.
- **Facts, Unresolved 7: "`KeyPair::from_pem` … unverified."** It exists and the tree uses it (`src/adapters/remote.rs:139`, `:146`). Reissuing a certificate over the stored key needs no new key API. The `time` types rcgen's validity fields take are not a direct dependency (`chrono` is, `Cargo.toml:37`); the plan builds the dates with `rcgen::date_time_ymd` from a `chrono` date.
- **Facts, Settled (subprotocol): "the server echoes the token protocol."** The plan echoes a fixed second protocol, `switchboard.v1`, which the page offers beside the token. WHATWG step 11.2 and RFC 6455 §4.1 are met (a protocol came back, and it is one the client sent), and the token is not repeated in a response header.

## The record

No new record kind, and `SCHEMA_VERSION` (`src/core/model.rs:12`, 16 today) and `VIEWS_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`:612`, 7 today) do not move.

A browser is one more `PairedDevice` in `devices.json` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96-107`), a file with no version, written by `Effect::SaveDevices`. Its name is the page's own `device_name` ("Safari on iPhone"), taken by `remote_pair` (`src/app.rs:3606`) and cut to 64 characters in `AppCore::new_device` (`src/core/remote.rs:166`). No `kind` field: the name is enough to tell a browser in the dialog (issue decision 6). Rehydration is unchanged: `IdentityLoaded` puts the devices back and a token is checked by hash on every request.

`identity.json` changes, because a browser checks names and dates the native clients never looked at. Today the certificate has no subjectAltName at all and rcgen's default validity (`make_identity`, `src/adapters/remote.rs:95-127`).

- `Identity` (`src/ports/remote.rs:26-42`) gains `certificate_names: Vec<String>` and `certificate_not_after: Option<SystemTime>`, both `#[serde(default)]`.
- `IDENTITY_SCHEMA_VERSION` (`src/ports/remote.rs:17`, 1 today) becomes the value in that file at implementation time, plus one, since a ticket landing in parallel may take the next number first. The identity loader has no version branch (`src/adapters/remote.rs:74`) and no `store::migrate` step applies: it is not a `model.rs` type. The defaults are the migration; an older build that loads the file and saves it drops the two fields, and the next launch of this build writes them again.
- A certificate made by `make_identity` and by the new `reissue_certificate(identity, key_pem, names, now)` carries: the SANs (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1` and `remote::local_address()` when there is one, as `iPAddress`), `serverAuth` EKU, `not_before` now and `not_after` 825 days out, and `is_ca` set explicitly (`BasicConstraints` path length 0), because the saved-file route below needs CA:true (Facts, Settled: code-server's iPad guide; Apple's 825-day and SAN rules). All set explicitly because the rcgen defaults are unverified (Facts, Unresolved 7). No `.local` name: Facts, Settled says it reaches Safari over mDNS but it was not tested on a device, so it is not a SAN.
- The key is reused, so `spki_sha256` and every pairing survive (§5: "a certificate reissued from the same key still verifies"). The reissue happens in `load_identity` (`src/app.rs:2780`), in the branch where the Keychain key matches `identity.spki_sha256`: when `certificate_names` differs from the wanted names, `certificate_not_after` is `None`, or it is under 30 days away. It saves through `services.remote.save_identity` directly, as `make_identity` does at `src/app.rs:2866-2875`, not through an action. That is deliberate: an action would emit `Effect::SaveIdentity`, whose arm rebinds the port when the listen setting differs from `remote_bound`, and `bind_remote` clears `remote_bound` first, so a reissue from inside a bind would recurse. A read-only instance does not reissue (it does not for `make_identity` either).

None of the host's signals change; the page speaks the protocol the headset speaks, and the page's one new read is `GET /api/v1/device`. Two additions on the connection:

- **The token on the WebSocket (issue decision 2).** `new WebSocket(url, ["switchboard.v1", token])`. `read_request` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:444`) reads `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` on an upgrade: when it lists `switchboard.v1` the request carries `subprotocol: Some("switchboard.v1")`, and any other item is the token, which goes into `bearer` when no `Authorization` header gave one. `respond_upgrade` (`:519`) writes `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: switchboard.v1` when the request offered it (Facts, Settled: a client that offers protocols fails the handshake if none is echoed). The base64url token is a legal `token` value (Facts, Settled: RFC 7230 `tchar`, RFC 6455 §4.2.2). Native clients keep the bearer header. **No cookie is set or read anywhere.** Reasons, each from Facts: cookies are not isolated by port, so every HTTPS service on the Mac would receive a `Secure` cookie (Settled); a `SameSite=Strict` cookie can be missing from a WebSocket in a restored Safari tab (Settled, WebKit 200345 and 232666); whether Chrome and Firefox send it (Unresolved 4) and whether `Secure` works on an IP host (Unresolved 5) are unanswered. The subprotocol route depends on none of them, so O3 (does it survive a Safari restore) changes nothing.
- **Where the token lives on the device.** `localStorage`, per origin, which is readable by any script on the origin; a cookie would not be. The plan's answer is that the only script is `/app.js` under `script-src 'self'`, and the page writes every host string with `textContent`, never `innerHTML`. That is the residual risk and the dialog text does not hide it. The page also stores the non-secret marker (`server_id`, `spki_sha256`, `device_id`).
- **`Origin` on upgrades (Facts, Settled: RFC 6455 §1.3, §4.2.2).** `read_request` also keeps `Origin` and `Host`. `remote_subscribe` (`src/app.rs:2723`) refuses with 403 `bad_origin` an upgrade whose `Origin` is present and is not `https://` plus the request's own `Host`. That accepts the IP, a hostname or loopback, whichever the page was opened by, and a request with no `Origin` (a native client). It runs after `authenticate`, so a stranger learns nothing. POSTs need no check: they need the `Authorization` header, which a cross-site page cannot send without a CORS preflight the host never answers.

One pair, for the saved-file route. Facts, Unresolved 1 (does iOS Safari offer a click-through at all) is conflicted, and Settled says a click-through does not carry `wss://` on iOS (WebKit 41419; code-server's guide). A phone that offers no click-through can reach nothing the host serves, so the certificate cannot be offered by the host's own port; it comes from the Mac.

- **Token (decision 2):** it travels in `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` and lives in `localStorage`. No cookie is set or read. The host checks `Origin` on upgrades.

  - Three paths are served: `/`, `/app.js` and `/app.css`. They are answered on the connection thread, with a strict CSP.
  - Each static reply closes its connection and has its own 60-per-minute window.
  - The unauthenticated pool stays at 4.

- **Left for the owner:** the plan sets the certificate's CA flag with path length 0 so an installed copy will be accepted. That lets a device that installs the file treat the Mac's key as a CA. It needs the owner's say-so, and it is listed at the end of the plan.
